issues.legal_issue: A protected tenant’s interest in premises may be inherited when the governing rental law treats a person continuing in possession after termination as a tenant and does not limit that interest to a personal right of occupation.
material_facts: The tenants died while their appeal against an eviction decree was pending, and their heirs sought to continue the appeal.

The governing law defined a tenant to include a person continuing in possession after termination of the tenancy, subject to its stated exclusion for a person against whom an eviction order or decree had been made.
The law’s restrictions on subletting applied to tenants as defined, supporting the conclusion that a protected tenant retained an interest in the premises.
issues.conclusion: The tenants’ interest in the premises was heritable, and their heirs were entitled to prosecute the pending appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The incidents of a protected tenancy must be determined from the governing statute, rather than imported from the English concept of statutory tenancy. Under sections 2(i) and 14 of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961, continued possession after termination was included in the definition of tenant, and the restriction on subletting applied to that defined class. The Court distinguished Anand Nivas (Private) Ltd. v. Anandji Kalyanji Pedhi and Jagdish Chander Chatterjee v. Sri Kishan, which proceeded on a different statutory basis and treated the protected tenant’s right as personal; it also referred to the English cases Roe v. Russell, Haskins v. Lewis, Keeves v. Dean and Boyer v. Warbey.

predicates.tenancy_appeal_after_tenant_death: A tenant died while an appeal concerning the tenancy or the right to remain in the premises was pending.
predicates.governing_law_includes_continuing_posses: The governing rental law treats a person continuing in possession after termination of the tenancy as a tenant, subject to the law’s stated limits.
predicates.subletting_restrictions_apply_to_that_te: The governing rental law applies its restrictions on subletting to the class of tenants that includes persons continuing in possession after termination.

issues.definition: When a tenant dies during a tenancy appeal and the governing law treats continuing possessors as tenants subject to the same subletting restrictions, the heirs may continue the appeal.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s acceptance of rent by cheque may be implied, making a cheque a valid tender when the circumstances do not indicate that cheque payment is unacceptable.
material_facts: The tenants tendered the arrears by cheque within the relevant time.
The landlord refused to accept the cheque.
The circumstances did not indicate that the parties had excluded payment by cheque.
issues.conclusion: The cheque amounted to a valid tender of rent, so the tenants could not be evicted on the asserted ground of non-payment.
issues.legal_principle: Rent is payable as a debt, ordinarily in cash or other legal tender, but the mode of payment may be altered by agreement. In contemporary society, an agreement to accept payment by cheque may reasonably be implied unless the circumstances indicate otherwise. A cheque sent in payment of a debt operates as a discharge if it is not dishonoured; where it is sent by post and met on presentation, payment is dated from posting.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_based_on_rent_nonpay: A landlord seeks eviction on the ground that the tenant failed to pay rent arrears.
predicates.rent_arrears_tendered_by_cheque_within_t: The tenant offered the rent arrears by cheque within the applicable time.
predicates.circumstances_do_not_exclude_cheque_paym: The circumstances of the parties’ dealings do not indicate that payment by cheque was unacceptable.

issues.definition: If a tenant timely tenders rent arrears by cheque in an eviction proceeding for non-payment, and the circumstances do not exclude cheque payment, the cheque is a valid tender.

issues.legal_issue: A court hearing a second appeal may set aside a factual finding that was reached by overlooking important and relevant evidence.
material_facts: The trial court rejected the landlords’ claim of bona fide need, relying in part on evidence that their income was sufficient only for their livelihood and was not sufficient even for their maintenance.
The first appellate court reversed that finding, reasoning that there was no evidence that the landlords lacked funds to start the proposed business.
The High Court found that the first appellate court had overlooked material evidence bearing on the landlords’ ability to start the business and restored the trial court’s finding.
issues.conclusion: The High Court acted within its jurisdiction in setting aside the first appellate court’s finding and restoring the dismissal of the eviction suit.
issues.legal_principle: A finding of fact reached by ignoring important and relevant evidence is bad in law. The Court relied on Radha Nath Seal v. Haripada Jana. It noted the parties’ reliance on Madan Lal Puri v. Sain Das Berry, Mattulal v. Radhey Lal and Sarvate T. B. v. Nemi Chand, but did not decide the apparent conflict between those decisions about whether a bona fide requirement finding is one of fact or a mixed question of law and fact.

predicates.second_appeal_from_factual_finding: A second appeal challenges a factual finding made by the lower appellate court.
predicates.lower_appellate_court_overlooked_materia: The lower appellate court reached its finding without considering important evidence relevant to the issue.

issues.definition: When a lower appellate court overlooks important evidence in making a factual finding challenged in a second appeal, the second appellate court may set that finding aside.
